column4: The section's named ف ج ر root is water breaking out through rock; this ayah says some stones let rivers burst from them (يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهُ ٱلْأَنْهَارُ), the exact image it develops.

The section pictures water breaking through stone; here Moses strikes a stone and twelve springs burst from it (فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا), giving the image a measured communal supply.
The section's rock-to-water image recurs when Moses strikes the rock and twelve springs gush (فَٱنۢبَجَسَتْ مِنْهُ); each group knows its drinking place, linking the release to allotted provision.
This is the section's own flood formulation: God makes the earth burst into springs (فَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا), and the waters meet over a matter already decreed, joining eruption to measure.

The section's w-d-y lexicon calls a valley a channel for a flood; here valleys run according to their capacity (سَالَتْ أَوْدِيَةٌ بِقَدَرِهَا), while swelling foam vanishes and what benefits people remains.

The section names the ف ج ر root both for bursting water and for fujūr, opening into sin; at the judgment the seas themselves are burst open (ٱلْبِحَارُ فُجِّرَتْ), making that physical and moral wording meet.
The section explicitly gives ف ج ر the secondary moral sense of opening into sins; this ayah names the wicked (ٱلْفُجَّارَ) and sets their Fire against the righteous' bliss in the preceding ayah.
The section's named ف ج ر branch is launching oneself into sin; this ayah says a person wants to sin ahead of himself (لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ), giving the moral sense as an act.

The section links a spring to water bursting forth; here God makes springs gush within the earth (فَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ ٱلْعُيُونِ) amid gardens of palms and grapes, showing the same release as cultivated abundance.

The section sets human demand for a river-filled garden against divinely given water; these deniers demand a garden with rivers running through it and that a spring be made to burst from the earth (تُفَجِّرَ لَنَا مِنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ يَنۢبُوعًا).

Where the section says the Quran gives its bursting spring to God's servants in the Garden, this ayah describes a spring (عَيْنًا) that those servants make gush as they wish (يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا), placing the same act in a setting of divine reward rather than a sign demanded from a messenger.
The section names ط غ ي for water exceeding its measure; this ayah uses the same root directly of the floodwater (طَغَى ٱلْمَاءُ) and says God carried people in the running ship.

The section's Ad scene turns a cloud they take for rain (هَٰذَا عَارِضٌ مُمْطِرُنَا) into a wind bearing painful punishment (رِيحٌ فِيهَا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ); the expected sweet water and actual scourge occupy one scene.

Hud tells Ad that turning back would bring rain pouring abundantly (يُرْسِلِ ٱلسَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُم مِّدْرَارًا); alongside the section's cloud that Ad mistakes for rain but receives as punishment, this shows the same sky's merciful alternative.

The section's Thamud carve rock at the valley and later increase فساد; Salih recalls their carving of mountain homes (تَنْحِتُونَ ٱلْجِبَالَ بُيُوتًا) and forbids being corruptors (مُفْسِدِينَ), directly joining their settlement and moral excess.

The section glosses ف س د as departure from balance and makes the land's and sea's excess audible in that corruption; this ayah says فساد has appeared on land and sea (فِى ٱلْبَرِّ وَٱلْبَحْرِ) through people's deeds, grounding the image in its consequences.

The section says فساد grows and things leave their proper measure; this destroyer spreads فساد on earth and ruins crops and offspring (يُهْلِكَ ٱلْحَرْثَ وَٱلنَّسْلَ), a concrete reversal of rain's yield.

The section's فساد is what leaves a thing balanced; this ayah forbids فساد on earth after its repair (بَعْدَ إِصْلَاحِهَا), setting destructive overflow against a restored land. Its next ayah, 7:57, supplies the rain and revival scene.

The section names rain as حَيَا because it revives earth after death; this ayah sends winds and clouds to dead land, brings forth fruit, then says God brings out the dead in the same way (كَذَٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ).
The section contrasts punishment poured from above with rain poured for food; this ayah uses the same ص ب ب verb for water (صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا), whose benefit appears in the following verses.
The section's water-benefit scene continues as God splits the earth open (شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا) after pouring water in 80:25; the next verses identify the food that grows from it.
After the section's rain poured and earth split in 80:25–26, this continuing list begins with grain (حَبًّا), a specific yield of the life-giving water.
The food list following the section's cited rain-and-split-earth pair names grapes (عِنَبًا), making the water's provision concrete.
The section's final ج ن ن dictionary note describes plant thickening; this continuing harvest list names dense gardens (حَدَائِقَ غُلْبًا), a close picture of that growth.
The section's rain is linked to growing food; in the continuation after 80:25–26 this ayah names olives and palms (زَيْتُونًا وَنَخْلًا) as further yield.
The section says measured rain yields food; the same post-rain list names fruit and pasture (فَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا), extending provision to people and animals.

The section reads restricted رزق as the humanly visible side of measured rain; the preceding crop list ends by calling its yield provision for people and livestock (مَّتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ).
The section names ق د ر for rain descending by measure; this ayah says water came down by measure (بِقَدَرٍ) and was settled in earth, while God remains able to take it away.
This ayah gives the section's measured-water claim directly: God sends water from the sky by measure (بِقَدَرٍ), revives a dead land, and says people will likewise be brought out.

The section links water over measure with human excess and measured rain with رزق; this ayah says unlimited provision would make people transgress on earth (لَبَغَوْا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ), while God sends it by measure.
The section names the dictionary usage of rain as رزق; this ayah locates people's provision in the sky (وَفِى ٱلسَّمَاءِ رِزْقُكُمْ), making the rain/provision link explicit.

The section points out that عَذَاب shares its named root with عَذْب, pleasant fresh water; this ayah sets fresh sweet water (عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ) against salty bitter water, sharpening the section's turn from expected drink to punishment.

The section links rain-revived earth to the raising of the dead; this ayah describes dead earth stirring, swelling and sprouting after rain (ٱهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ وَأَنۢبَتَتْ) before likening resurrection to it.

The section makes rain a provision that revives the earth; this ayah says water is sent to revive dead land and give drink to many people and animals (نُّسْقِيَهُۥ مِمَّا خَلَقْنَآ أَنْعَٰمًا وَأَنَاسِىَّ كَثِيرًا).

The section names rain حَيَا for restoring earth after death; this ayah tells the reader to look at the traces of God's mercy in rain and at how He revives earth after its death (يُحْىِ ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَآ).
The section's rain makes dead ground live; this ayah shows humbled land becoming stirred and growing when water falls, then calls that revival a sign of God's power to revive the dead.
The section moves from rain to its food and garden yield; this ayah calls the water blessed (مَآءً مُّبَٰرَكًا) and says it brings forth gardens and grain, tying rain directly to produce.
The section's rain-to-garden image continues in this ayah's tall date palms with clustered fruit (نَّخْلٍ بَاسِقَٰتٍ لَّهَا طَلْعٌ نَّضِيدٌ), a concrete growth from rain-fed land.

The section connects rain, رزق and life's return; this ayah calls the crops provision for servants and says the same rain revives dead land (رِّزْقًا لِّلْعِبَادِ وَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِۦ بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا).
The section's rain becomes plants and fruit; this ayah sends water from the sky, brings out varied growth, grain and clusters of dates, and names its ripe fruit as a sign for reflection.
The section's rain supplies life and provision; this ayah sends water from the sky for drink and plant growth, placing both needs in one scene.
The section follows rain into food and gardens; this continuation says water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes and every kind of fruit (يُنۢبِتُ لَكُم بِهِ ٱلزَّرْعَ), making the provision concrete.
The section traces water to living growth; this ayah says God sends water from the sky and brings out diverse kinds of plants (أَزْوَٰجًا مِّن نَّبَاتٍ شَتَّىٰ).
The section's plant growth is a provision; the continuation tells people to eat and pasture their livestock, directly showing the crop's use.
The section's ص ب ب image is water poured from above; this ayah calls rain pouring water (مَآءً ثَجَّاجًا) from the clouds, followed by grain and gardens in 78:15–16.
The section's poured rain leads to food; this ayah names grain (حَبًّا) brought forth from the rain scene begun in 78:14.
The section's ج ن ن note connects the garden to dense plant growth; following rain and grain, this ayah names thick, intertwined gardens (جَنَّٰتٍ أَلْفَافًا).

The section's lexicon says رَجْع can mean rain that falls, returns and falls again; this ayah swears by the sky of recurring return (وَٱلسَّمَآءِ ذَاتِ ٱلرَّجْعِ), giving that rain cycle a direct formulation.
Noah tells his people that repentance would bring abundant rain (يُرْسِلِ ٱلسَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُم مِّدْرَارًا); beside the section's destructive flood, this gives the same rain a merciful outcome.
The section ties rain to gardens and provision; continuing Noah's promise, this ayah links rain with wealth, children, gardens and rivers (جَنَّٰتٍ وَيَجْعَل لَّكُمْ أَنْهَٰرًا).
The section turns rain from punishment to mercy and food; this ayah says God sends rain after people despair (مِن بَعْدِ مَا قَنَطُوا) and spreads His mercy, an explicit reversal of the feared cloud.

The section names Ad among those whose excess brings punishment; this reminder says Ad had gardens and springs (فِى جَنَّٰتٍ وَعُيُونٍ), showing the land and water abundance they received before their downfall.

The section recalls Noah's flood as earth bursting into springs; at its close God commands earth to swallow its water and sky to stop (ٱبْلَعِى مَآءَكِ وَيَٰسَمَآءُ أَقْلِعِى), placing a boundary on overflow.
This opens the flood scene continued by the section's cited 54:12: the sky's gates are opened with pouring water (بِمَآءٍ مُّنْهَمِرٍ), supplying the downpour that meets the earth's springs.
This is Hud's warning to Ad, the scene that leads to their rain-cloud misreading in 46:24; its contribution is the threatened punishment already rejected before they call the cloud rain.
The section's Noah flood has an onset marked by the oven boiling over (فَارَ ٱلتَّنُّورُ); 54:12 then depicts earth bursting into springs, so this ayah adds the deluge's first signal.
In Noah's flood, a wave separates his son from the ark and he drowns; this gives the section's water-overflow scene a human consequence beyond the meeting of waters in 54:12.
The section recalls Noah's flood; here the ark moves amid waves like mountains (فِى مَوْجٍ كَٱلْجِبَالِ), making the scale of the flood visible.
The section names Pharaoh with the tyrants beneath the poured scourge; this ayah shows Pharaoh overtaken by drowning in the sea (أَدْرَكَهُ ٱلْغَرَقُ), a water-borne punishment in his own story.
The section groups Pharaoh with those who exceeded limits and received punishment; here his people are drowned in the sea (فَأَغْرَقْنَٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ), making water itself the judgment.

The section's named fujūr is the moral opening into sin; this ayah names the soul's wickedness (فُجُورَهَا) beside its godwariness (وَتَقْوَىٰهَا), clarifying the moral sense against its water-bursting sense.
The section explicitly gives ف ج ر a moral sense; this ayah calls the wrongdoers al-fujjār (ٱلْفُجَّارِ) and places their record in Sijjīn, another concrete use of the named secondary sense.
The section notes the shared dictionary root between عَذَاب and عَذْب; this ayah contrasts fresh sweet water (عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ) with salty water, giving the sweet-water side of that lexical turn.
The section's spring image is water forced into a channel; these Gardens contain two bubbling springs (عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ), a specific gushing-water counterpart in paradise.
The section joins a spring and a Garden; this Garden description puts two running springs (عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ) among its rewards, pairing water with the garden named at the section's end.
The section's Ad mistake turns a cloud taken for rain into painful wind; this ayah describes clouds joined and spread until rain and hail descend, showing the actual rain-bearing face of such clouds.
The section says life is rain that revives land; this ayah joins lightning that inspires fear and hope to water from the sky that revives the earth after death, holding threat and mercy together.
The section's cloud carries either rain or punishment; this ayah depicts God driving clouds, spreading them and bringing rain out of them, the rain-bearing scene that 30:50 calls a trace of mercy.
Before the rain in 30:48, people had been in despair; this makes the section's unexpected rain and its opposite, the cloud that becomes punishment, a specific contrast of expectation.
The section's rain revives dead earth; this ayah describes winds driving clouds to a dead land and God reviving earth after its death, a repeated direct formulation.
The section links rain to life returning to the earth; this ayah names water sent from the sky as provision that brings the earth back to life after death (فَأَحْيَا بِهِ ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا).
The section's rain is what revives the earth; this ayah asks who sends water from the sky and gives life to dead land, then names God's answer, a repeated formulation of that sign.

The section's dictionary note makes rain the life of dead earth; this ayah states the image's resulting claim directly, that God gives life to the earth after its death (يُحْيِى ٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا).

The section says measured rain corresponds to measured provision; this parable gives a garden on high ground that yields double after a heavy shower or still yields after a light drizzle, showing productive outcomes at different rain amounts.
The section names rain as رزق and follows it to food; this ayah sends water from the sky, brings forth fruits, and calls them provision for people (رِزْقًا لَّكُمْ).

The section says a person mistakes narrowed رزق for humiliation; this ayah says God expands and restricts provision, then contrasts worldly rejoicing with the smallness of this life beside the Hereafter.

The section's reading of 89:15–16 treats abundance and restriction as God's measure of provision; this ayah states that the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it (يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ).
The section rejects reading restricted provision as humiliation; this ayah asks whether people know God expands or restricts provision as He wills, identifying the same measure as a sign.
The section's rain-return image in 86:11 is followed by earth with a crack (وَٱلْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ ٱلصَّدْعِ), returning the reader to its opening image of a split through which water emerges.
